nameStory: The name "fulmar" comes from the Old Norse words "fúll" (foul) and "már" (gull), meaning "foul gull." This rather unflattering name refers to their ability to projectile vomit a smelly, oily substance when threatened. Despite the name suggesting they're gulls, fulmars are actually petrels - members of an entirely different bird family!
description: Northern Fulmars are chunky seabirds that spend most of their lives gliding over the open ocean. They're about the size of a large gull but have a distinctive thick neck and stubby appearance. These hardy birds come in two color forms: a light version with white head and body plus gray wings, or a darker gray version found in Arctic populations. You'll rarely see them close to shore in New England, as they prefer the deep waters far offshore.

idTips.label: Tube-shaped nostrils
idTips.description: Look for distinctive tube-like nostrils on top of the thick, hooked bill - these nasal tubes are clearly visible and unique among seabirds you'll see in New England waters

idTips.label: Stiff-winged flight
idTips.description: Flies with wings held stiffly straight out, gliding and banking over waves without much flapping - very different from the flexible wing-beats of gulls

idTips.label: Thick, stubby build
idTips.description: Has a chunky, compact body with a thick neck and large head, giving it a more robust appearance than the sleeker gulls

idTips.label: Multi-plated bill
idTips.description: The thick bill appears to be made of several distinct horny plates rather than smooth like a gull's - you can often see the plate divisions if viewing through binoculars

idTips.label: Color variations
idTips.description: May appear as a light bird (white body, gray wings) or uniformly gray, with many intermediate shades possible between these two extremes

habitat: Northern Fulmars are found far offshore in New England's deep ocean waters, typically many miles from land. They prefer the cold, nutrient-rich waters over the continental shelf and beyond. In New England, you're most likely to spot them from whale-watching boats or during offshore birding trips, as they rarely venture close to shore.

seasonality.spring: More likely to be seen as they follow fishing boats and whales offshore during spring migration periods. Look for them during offshore birding trips in April and May.
seasonality.summer: Present in offshore waters but dispersed widely over the ocean. Summer whale-watching trips may encounter them, especially in areas with active feeding.
seasonality.fall: Peak time for sightings from shore-based locations during storm events, when strong winds may push them closer to land. Late fall storms occasionally bring them into harbors.
seasonality.winter: Least likely to be observed from New England waters, as many birds move to more southern offshore areas. Any winter sightings are noteworthy.

funFact: When threatened, Northern Fulmars can projectile vomit a foul-smelling stomach oil up to six feet with remarkable accuracy - and this oily substance is so effective at matting the feathers of attacking birds that it can actually cause them to lose their waterproofing and drown!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with gulls due to similar size and some color patterns, but fulmars have distinctive tube-shaped nostrils on top of their bills (gulls have simple nostril slits), much stiffer wing posture in flight, and a chunkier build. Memory trick: "Tubes on top = not a gull!"
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "foul gulls" by Norse sailors and resembling gulls in some ways, Northern Fulmars are actually petrels - close relatives of albatrosses. This is a classic example of convergent evolution, where unrelated species develop similar appearances due to similar lifestyles, leading to naming confusion that persists today.
compareHints: Northern Fulmars are the only fulmar species you'll encounter in New England waters, but they're most similar to other petrels and shearwaters in their flight style and offshore habitat. Unlike the sleeker shearwaters that skim just above the waves, fulmars fly with a more erratic, banking flight pattern at various heights above the water. Their chunky build and tube-shaped nostrils distinguish them from all other petrel family members in the region.
